ResponsesInList.Title: Thinkbot menace
ResponsesInList.Text: I was surprised not to find "Thinkbot" in the forums here. Or is it something everybody knows, I'm just a late victim? It had happened more than once that the number of Apache processes ramp up by about 100 withing a time period of 80-90 minutes and the number of MySQL ( MariaDB ) threads climb vertically by about 50. The culprit is a bot visiting (scraping) publicly readable Moodle pages, mostly site announcements. The user agent is "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Thinkbot/0.5.8;  +In_the_test_phase,_if_the_Thinkbot_brings_you_trouble,_please_block_its_IP_address._Thank_you.)" What surprised me was how repeatedly visiting say forum posts, how the number of DB threads go up. Then only realized that the requests come from many different IP addresses, so the system starts different DB sessions! After the 80-90 wave it stops, the server comes back to normal quickly. Still, it is a big annoyance. How do the others handle this, other than blocking the IP addresses - if I count them over all the "waves" that's more than 100.

ResponsesInList.Title: Thinkbot menace
ResponsesInList.Text: ThinkBot targets.  Can re-call having bouts with them but none recently.   It probably thinks my sites don't have any useful info! Got a WAF ? ... like CloudFlare? Can you determine how many ip's or range of ip's from which the traffic comes? fgrep Thinkbot /var/logs/* or something like that. Could block at network layer ... if IP's are servers - think you can tell by whois ipaddress sudo ufw deny from xx.xx.xx.xx/xx Could block the class c, b of IP addresses with the subnet mask ... the /xx above /24 255.255.255.0 - class c /16 is 255.255.0.0 - class b I've got quite a list! The bot id's as Thinkbot right?   Could try Apache Example (using .htaccess): RewriteEngine On RewriteCond %{HTTP_USER_AGENT} ThinkBot [NC] RewriteRule .* - [F,L] Guess Security experts are taking a well deserved day off! 'SoS', Ken

ResponsesInList.Title: Thinkbot menace
ResponsesInList.Text: Follow up ... forgot I had this ... mod_evasive for apache. Has setting for thresholds - number of hits from a single IP address - as well as a whitelist (your own server IP and whatever workstation you use normally).  Threshold is reached, IP address is blocked. Restart of apache clears blocks. If you check apache status ... the info will show the IP's blocked by mod_evasive.   Ran into this when learning how to install moodle 5.1. 'SoS', Ken

ResponsesInList.Title: Thinkbot menace
ResponsesInList.Text: Am not sure anyone is gonna find something that works 100% of the time.   But, knowing you have the ability to temporarily block an IP or range of IP's is, IMHO , a good thing to do. The blocks I setup are not permanent and if I reboot the server that list is cleared and am starting over.   Thus, when I block, I have the script write to a reloadblocks file and can reload them all again. Those 'institute buildings' have static IP's ... put them in mod_evasive whitelist.   Those are IP's that you control, right? I help admin moodle servers for K12.  K12 sites have siblings from same family ... thus same IP address if they access from home.  Older sibling, home on holiday break, decides to test their new knowledge from buddies at college on the Moodle server.  Best time to hack a K12 box is on a holiday break.  The IT staff at the K12 entity is also on holiday ... and they figure no one is watching.   Easy to spot as their is literally no traffic from the private IP network and what kiddo on holiday wants to do any work?   None! The above event has happened more than once .... I block the IP.  Say nothing about that action.   Upon return from holiday, younger sibling attempts to access and cannot.  Parent reports to IT folks, IT folks contact me, I take the block off. I have kept the logs of the activity so I could provide that info if asked ... send those logs to IT folks.   They agree that it should have been blocked.  IT contacts parent to inform ... older sibling got a stern talking to from Parent.    Sometimes younger folks are just not aware of the potential serious consequences. Anyhoo, mov_evasive fits my situation ... and is better than nothing ... IMHO. Another story ... entity in Africa ... having issues reaching their moodle server ... there is nothing wrong with the moodle server.  Checked DNS and found they were using a WAF called SiteGuard .. no one at the entity was aware they were using SiteGuard and afraid to remove it ... SiteGuard does the same as CloudFlare - DNS trickery.   After waiting a week for the entity to make a decision ... decided to test to prove to them that the issue was SiteGuard. Changed DNS for the moodle server to point directly to the moodle server rather than SiteGuard ... fixed!   And they didn't suffer from any attack ... actually the issue was 2 fold and had an internal factor ... had the webshell plugin installed in their moodle and 15 persons had admin level access ... 5 of whom were students!  Removed plugin, demoted students to students.   Fixed!   (Imagine that!) 'SoS', Ken

ResponsesInList.Title: Eliminating World Writable Files
ResponsesInList.Text: My organization has started using Rapid7 InsightVM to scan our servers for vulnerabilities. We have Moodle 4.4.6+ (Build: 20250214) installed on a stand alone Linux server (no other users/apps). The scan has identified world writable files as a security risk. After reviewing the links below, I've decided to modify the files and directories References : https://docs.moodle.org/404/en/Security_recommendations#Running_Moodle_on_a_dedicated_server https://docs.moodle.org/404/en/Installing_Moodle#Download_and_copy_files_into_place https://docs.moodle.org/404/en/Installation_quick_guide#Install_Moodle_code Ran the following commands on my server: Change permissions for moodle app code: `sudo find /var/www/moodle -type d -exec chmod 0755 {} \;` `sudo find /var/www/moodle -type f -exec chmod 0644 {} \;` 0755 (dirs): Allows the owner full access and group/others to read and enter the directory. 0644 (files): Owner can read/write, group and others can read — no write access for anyone else. Change permissions for moodle app data: `sudo find /var/www/moodledata -type d -exec chmod 0750 {} \;` `sudo find /var/www/moodledata -type f -exec chmod 0640 {} \;` 0750 (dirs): Allows the owner full access and group members to read/enter. 0640 (files): Owner can read/write, group can read — no access for "others." After doing this, existing files and directories were no longer world writable, but moodle continued to produce new world writable files. So I then made the following changes to moodle’s config file, as well as modifying apache’s `umask` setting. /var/www/html/config.php Originally: `$CFG->directorypermissions = 02777;` Changed to: `$CFG->directorypermissions = 02750;` 02750 - Apache + group can read/exec, Some group-based read access is needed Also, added this near the top of config.php: `umask(0027);` This ensures that Moodle uses the correct umask even if the server is misconfigured. /etc/apache2/envvars Add this at the end (or edit if it already exists): `umask 0027` Any new files or directories created by Apache processes will have permissions that do not allow world access. However, moodle is still creating world writable files (most recent identified was /var/www/moodledata/localcache/di/CompiledContainer.php (-rw-rw-rw-) While looking into this, I've come across one or two posts claiming that the entire moodledata directory should be world writable. I don't think this is correct based on the other links I have shared above (and many more that I read regarding "hardening" moodle). So my questions now are as follows: Can someone confirm if this directory should be world writable? If yes, please explain how moodle protects the files in there and the server from malicious behaviour (I will need this information to submit and exception request to my security team) If no, how can I prevent moodle from creating new world writable files? Can someone point me to official documentation that deals with directory and file creation permissions? I followed an assortment of guides when installing, but mostly the Step-by-step Installation Guide for Ubuntu - MoodleDocs . It briefly mentions changing permissions after install, but doing that (as I did) still results in world writable files Thank you all for any assistance you can provide.

ResponsesInList.Title: Eliminating World Writable Files
ResponsesInList.Text: A thorough research! You can solve the mystery yourself starting from the first principles. They are: 1. The web server processes belong to a certain user and a group. For example in Apache2 under Debian Linux, they are in the /etc/apache2/envvars. export APACHE_RUN_USER=www-data, export APACHE_RUN_GROUP=www-data. 2. Those web server processes need read access to the Moodle code, in your case /var/www/moodle/ (and everything below that). Yes, only _read_ access. 3. Those web server processes need write access to the "moodledata" directory, in your case /var/www/moodledata/. I repeat, _write_ access (and obviously read access too). Usually you give Moodle an empty moodledata directory and from there on Moodle manages moodledata/ on its own. I know, you know this, but to eliminate a common misconception: The "everyone" group in Unix, what you call the World, is not the 8 billion world population nor the 5 billion of them having web access, rather all the other shell user accounts of the server that runs Moodle (more accurately, the web server that powers it). P.S. It just occurred to me that, if you delegated the "research" to those odd characters like ChatGPT, etc., it is not a crime, but a courtesy to mention that.

Why?   In a git acquired 4.5.latest code directory there are  69734 files/folders ... anyone of which could have something inserted ... not all scanners will  find them.   Plus, a file that looks like it belongs, doesn't! I'd highly recommend acquiring the new moodle code via git versioning.   Why?   Git knows about the byte size of every file in the repo ... and during a git pull to acquire new code, if any file doesn't match the known byte size, git will whoopie! WP in close proximity to Moodles can be done, and they can even talk to one another, but that's something to keep an eye on as a compromised WP site could find a way to compromise the moodle code. ResponsesInList.Title: Hide allowed domains in email-base self-registration
ResponsesInList.Text: We are encouraging our users (mostly teachers and pedagogical consultants) to connect to Moodle using OAuth2, but due to restrictions with some school districts not everyone has that option available. I set up "Email-based self-registration" with a whitelist of allowed domains. This works perfectly with ONE exception... I would like to hide the list of allowed domains so that bad actors can't bootstrap their way in using a spoofed email. I can't find a setting for this. Any suggestions?

ResponsesInList.Title: Hide allowed domains in email-base self-registration
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Robert! It's great to see you exploring the security options for your Moodle! I understand the concern about hiding the list of allowed domains for self-registration by email, to prevent malicious people from using a fake email to discover which domains are accepted. The good news is that you can adjust this directly in the Moodle code. I'll explain how to do it without any complications! 😄 What you need to do is modify a line in the `moodlelib.php` file. The line that needs to be modified displays the allowed domains when a user tries to register an email that's not on the list. So, what we’ll do is hide this list, making the system more secure. Here’s the step-by-step guide: Access the `moodlelib.php` file located in the `lib/` folder of your Moodle. Look for this code: `return get_string('emailonlyallowed', '', $CFG->allowemailaddresses);` See the Code on GitHub to search in your Moodle. To hide the list of allowed domains, replace that line with: `return get_string('emailonlyallowed', '', "");` Save the changes to the file. This small modification will prevent the list of domains from being displayed, leaving only the error message without revealing which domains are allowed. That way, anyone trying to use a fake email won't have access to this information. If you follow these steps, your Moodle will be even more secure for your users. I hope this resolves your issue! If you need anything, I'm here to help! 😎 We're in this together! Don’t hesitate to come back if you need anything else! Eduardo Kraus Innovation and new products

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Hide allowed domains in email-base self-registration
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Robert! There is a solution that is simpler than the previous one. Just remove the `{$a}` from the string responsible for displaying the list of allowed domains. Go to the section `Site administration` >> `Language` >> `Language customization` . On the customization screen, search for the string called `emailonlyallowed` . Save your changes. After that, the list of allowed domains will no longer be displayed during the registration process, preventing malicious users from attempting to manipulate the information. I hope this helps! We're always here for anything you need. If you need anything, just reach out! 😊 Eduardo Kraus Innovation and new products

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Hide allowed domains in email-base self-registration
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Robert, As Eduardo has pointed out, the allowed domains form part of the standard validation error, so there is no way to remove them without modifying the code. However, bad actors should still not be able to access your site even with that information. Email based self registration uses a confirmation step, which requires access to the email account to receive the confirmation link/token. Someone fabricating an email in the signup form won't have access to an email account at the address they have used, so should not be able to activate their account or log into the site.

ResponsesInList.Title: CVE-2025-1094 - Moodle is affected?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi I have a working Moodle on postgresql 16.6 Unfortunately, but I can't upgrade postgres in the near future. I wonder if this vulnerability can affect the security of Moodle? I have performed an analysis: CVE-2025-1094: https://www.postgresql.org/support/security/CVE-2025-1094/ Function Purpose: Postgre SQL provides functions such as PQescapeLiteral(), PQescapeIdentifier(), PQescapeString() and PQescapeStringConn() to “escape” (i.e. correctly handle) strings entered by users. In this way, they protect against so-called SQL injection - a situation in which a malicious user could inject additional, unauthorized SQL commands. The problem: In certain cases, when an application uses the result of these functions to build SQL queries (e.g. for an interactive psql terminal or command-line tools), improper neutralization may not work. As a result, a malicious user can manipulate the input data to insert their own SQL fragments into the query. Coding context : Specifically, the vulnerability occurs when specific encoding sets are used - for example, when the client's encoding is BIG5 and the server 's is one of EUC_TW or MULE_INTERNAL. It is with these configurations that the functions fail to fully neutralize characters. In my opinion, Moodle, as a system written in PHP, does not directly call functions such as PQescapeLiteral(), PQescapeIdentifier(), PQescapeString() or PQescapeStringConn(). Instead, Moodle uses the database abstraction layer and PHP extensions (such as pgsql or PDO_PGSQL) What do you think about it?

ResponsesInList.Title: Access to Moodle with SSO and manual enrolment
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi there, I'm wanting to pick some brains 😀 we have a Moodle site which we have set up for O365 SSO which is fine for our staff and students as they have O365 accounts. However, some of our departments would like to allow access to non-students as we would like to offer some free to access community type courses. My thoughts would be to open up manual enrolments as well as SSO - would this be classed as a guest access? Can those with manually added accounts still be classed as authorised users? Or would it be advisable to create a custom role (at the system level?) for these users which would still allow them to participate in the courses/ activities but not access any of our 'normal' and fee paying courses. Any help/advice greatly appreciated. Mel

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Access to Moodle with SSO and manual enrolment
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Mel, there are many ways you can grant access to courses for other users outside of SSO. In my experience the key criteria to handle this are administrative load and amount of extra accounts. Also, very important to remember is that the way a user comes into the moodle (usually, unless otherwise configured) does NOT have any bearing on the roles of the user within moodle. If a user logs in via SSO, they are an "authenticated user" in moodle and if their account gets added manually by an admin they are "they are an "authenticated user" in moodle" and if they register themselves via email they are an "authenticated user" in moodle... authentication =/= role. If you have only few users and enough time, then it is no problem to simply register the users manually, meaning an admin adds the users to moodle. They are then users like any other in moodle. Which courses they can access depends on the enrolement methods of the specific course. Additionally, these new accounts can be enroled manually into any course (and assigned roles in the course). If you want to register only a few people manually and have them only as viewing guest and not participating in the course, it'd be a good idea to create a role (maybe based on the guest role), configure it and assign it in the course context . Second, if those are too many users to manually add and manage, you can open up E-Mail-based self-registration for your moodle. However, I do not recommend doing this lightly without thinking about user data and course data protection and spam protection. At some point it usually is necessary to put in the breaks and cut of untethered access. Another method would be to enable Guest Access globally and then add Guest Enrolement to the course that should be open to guests. However, that's only in case you want ANYONE (worldwide) and without a registered account to be able to access the course. It is possible to configure a passwort though. If you set one, you'd have to give it to the people who are interested via email or any other way and then they can view the course. Mind that they all are only logged as "guest" and get the default "guest" role, which means only reading access and no participation (in default, very much depends on your config though). Just my two cents, I hope I could help a bit. Best, Connie

ResponsesInList.Title: Moodle Version Disclosure In Scan Tools
ResponsesInList.Text: How can I hide Moodle version details from being detected by scan tools like ImmuniWeb, especially when it still reveals version details even after adjusting headers to hide the information?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle Version Disclosure In Scan Tools
ResponsesInList.Text: It looks like they are using fingerprinting rather than any specific piece of data to analyse that information. That might be using JS library versions and page structures as part of this which is not possible to hide. This is a bit of a guess without knowing more about how they are fingerprinting.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle Version Disclosure In Scan Tools
ResponsesInList.Text: For the reasons Brett mentioned, among others, there's probably no way to 100% hide this. One thing to check would be the docs on hiding internal paths, which helps remove access to some of the information that might be used. You can find the docs for Apache here: https://docs.moodle.org/en/Apache#Hiding_internal_paths - there's also equivalent docs on their own pages for other web servers (eg nginx hiding internal files ).

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle Version Disclosure In Scan Tools
ResponsesInList.Text: Using the latest version of Moodle won't help achieving PCI/DSS compliance. The reported version (4.3.8) is fine to use as long as your server is properly patched, configured, and secured with multiple layers of protection such as web application firewalls, IDS, IPS, honeypots, proxy servers, and other scan/attack prevention mechanisms. Moodle is simply a web app that excels at what it was designed to do, and it has been doing the job well for over 20 years. On the other hand, a poorly configured, unprotected server will allow scanners to identify back-end software in detail, but this isn't Moodle's fault. Once your server is properly configured, any "wrong" step by a scanner should trigger your defense mechanisms to block malicious IPs, so there's no need to "hide" anything. But if you really want to try hiding this information, focus on writing rules that block direct access to (.txt) and (.md) files. Good luck!

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle Version Disclosure In Scan Tools
ResponsesInList.Text: To be clear Moodle does not claim PCI/DSS complaince in any way. That is a standard that applies to credit card payments industry and is a very different thing to what Moodle is used for.

ResponsesInList.Text: Follow-on question, can we be confident that the rewrite rules given in Security recommendations will hide everything that doesn't need to be public in /lib/?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Location of third party PHP libs
ResponsesInList.Text: For Catalyst plugins - we use the folder ".extlib" to put these into - it's not an official guideline, but it allows to have a rule to block all content within .extlib folders from being web accessible. eg: https://github.com/catalyst/moodle-auth_saml2/tree/MOODLE_39_STABLE/.extlib IDEA-75 is in the Moodle Roadmap for exploring a restructure of the codebase to allow for us to better control what code should be web-accessible, so it's possible that one day Moodle will allow us to control this a bit better

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Location of third party PHP libs
ResponsesInList.Text: When adding third-party PHP libraries to your setup, it’s ideal to keep them outside of the web-accessible `html/` directory for security. A common approach is to use a dedicated directory within your server , like `/var/www/vendor`, or within `moodledata` if it won’t interfere with Moodle’s data processing. Avoid placing libraries in `html/lib` directly, as they could be exposed if rewrite rules fail. Instead, you could place them in a `vendor` directory protected by rewrite rules. If you need more guidance on structuring third-party libraries, check out best practices from Google on secure PHP deployments.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: 15749 hits in 24 hours on the styles_debug.php
ResponsesInList.Text: Is mod_remoteip a plugin to moodle? Do you have the 'designer mode' turned on? The attacks started before you made the move to CloudFlare.   More than likely, those were conducted using IP address of your server and not FQDN. Try this your self from a work station: https://REALIPADDRESSOFSERVER/mod/readme.txt with FireFox , one will have to make an exception to view as the cert is tied to FQDN, but that URL will display. The theme is commercial .... so if this is really theme related, you need to communicate with support for the theme directly. You have AlmaLinux 8.   It's firewall has a drop zone.   Any iP address in the drop zone will be denied access to server without replying to request back to the IP address that requested with a browser code. I have a script called 'slogs': echo 'One param.'; echo 'Given: '$1 echo 'Paused ... press ENTER to continue searching logs.'; read $keypress; echo 'access_log'; fgrep $1 /var/log/httpd/access_log echo 'ssl_error_log'; fgrep $1 /var/log/httpd/ssl_error_log echo 'ssl_access_log'; fgrep $1 /var/log/httpd/ssl_access_log echo 'error_log'; fgrep $1 /var/log/httpd/error_log echo 'secure log'; fgrep $1 /var/log/secure When I see an IP up to no good, I'll run the above to see what specifically they are attempting to access. If I decide too much ... I have another script that checks that IP: whois on that IP should show CIDR and yet another that blocks that IP or the CIDR: firewall-cmd --zone=drop --add-source=$1 I don't make the drop zone entry permanent so on reboots that rule is cleared out. Once that is applied to the firewall, my server goes dark to that IP or range of IP addresses if using CIDR.  If I see that the logs show a server IP, I think 'bot' ... and block. It's not automated ... not sure that would be a good idea to do that. The whois info should also give you an abuse email address ... consider sending. a 'Cease and Desist' message along with a clip of logs to that address. My 2 cents. 'SoS', Ken

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Allowed Email Domains
ResponsesInList.Text: For anybody else wondering how to do this here is how I did it. The text is stored in the language pack for Moodle `lang/en/moodle.php` and is called `emailonlyallowed` . To edit it from the command line edit the line `$string['emailonlyallowed'] = 'This email cannot be used. Allowed email domains are: {$a}.';` to read `$string['emailonlyallowed'] = 'This email cannot be used. Allowed email domains are: {$a}.';` $a is the string that contains the list of email addresses that you want to hide. So if yo're not using English the text will be different but the variable name, which is what you want to hide, will be the same. This change will need to be made after each update. Note that Moodle caches these strings so your browser may not show the changes immediately. To disable the caches, in order to test, navigate to Site Administration > General > Language > Language Settings and uncheck Cache language menu and Cache all language strings . Re-enable once the changes are show in your browser on the signup page. To do it from the UI navigate to Site Administration > General > Language > Language Customisation . Choose your language and select Open Language Pack for editing . Once it's loaded click continue and choose moodle.php . In the search field called String identifier enter the text emailonlyallowed and click show strings. Change the text to "This email cannot be used.", ensuring there is no reference to the $a variable and click Save Changes to the language pack . This change will need to be made after each update but the export/import options will help here.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How to prevent cheating by using a browser extension?
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello, Mihail! 😊 I completely understand your concern about cheating during Moodle quizzes, especially with the use of these browser extensions like 'SyncShare'. It can definitely be a headache to maintain the integrity of assessments, particularly when dealing with young students in competitions. First, let's take a deep breath, because I have some practical tips that can help mitigate these problems without requiring super complex or costly solutions! 💡 Shuffle questions and answers : An effective feature that Moodle itself offers is the ability to shuffle both the questions and the answer options. This way, even if an extension tries to collect statistics on the answers, they won’t be as useful since the options will always be changing places. To do this, when creating or editing your quiz, simply enable the "shuffle questions" and "shuffle answers" options. This will already make it harder for anyone trying to cheat! Create larger question banks : Another way to frustrate these extensions is to work with a larger question bank and configure the quiz to randomly select a subset of questions for each student. This ensures that each student sees a different set of questions, making it more difficult for the extension or even groups of students to share answers. 🌟 Monitor suspicious behaviors : Moodle has a very robust logging system. You can track access, identify abnormal response times (such as students answering a question in seconds), and even restrict the number of accesses by IP. This helps to identify suspicious patterns, especially in important quizzes like competitions. Explore more advanced solutions : I understand that you mentioned the Safe Exam Browser (SEB) isn’t a viable option for all users, and I agree with that. You could reserve SEB for more critical cases or allow only certain students with easier installation access to use it at specific times. 😊 Blocking extensions via code : The solution you suggested of blocking the extension directly in the Moodle code is very interesting, but as you mentioned, it's more complicated and requires advanced technical knowledge in programming. A more practical alternative might be to restrict the use of certain browsers during quizzes or use third-party plugins to monitor behavior during the test. Check out this post here: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/75312160/check-my-users-to-see-if-my-extension-is-installed These tips should go a long way in reducing the use of cheating extensions, but it’s always good to remember that, unfortunately, there isn’t a 100% cheat-proof solution. A combination of various strategies, like the ones I’ve mentioned, will certainly make life harder for the “cheaters”! 😎 I hope this helps! If you have any further questions, we’re always here to assist and ensure your experience with Moodle keeps getting better. 🚀✨ Eduardo Kraus Professor / Programmer / Passionate about Moodle / Innovation and New Products

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Trying to fight fake account spam / shared list of Denied email domains
ResponsesInList.Text: Networking comes before Application ... application here is moodle. So attempting to block, etc. at the application level means the bots etc. are already knocking at your door and the situation is making your application work harder (moodle is 'heavy' enough without the added). So question: are you hosted on a VPS where you have root access? Reason asked, modern day servers have a firewall of their own that can used to deny any access to  the server via the NIC (the network interface card).   Can deny a single IP or a range of IP addresses. Rather than looking at emal addresses, look at server access logs for events involved and the IP address that event came from.  You might notice it's not a bunch but a few IP addresses. It's a process using different cli only tools to discover those IP addresses and I'd rather not spend a lot of time describing IF you don't have a VPS and root! 'SoS', Ken

ResponsesInList.Title: Content-Security-Policy (CSP) parameters for Moodle 4.1.8
ResponsesInList.Text: Request for guidance on Content-Security-Policy (CSP) parameters for Moodle 4.1.8 on Linux Platform (e.g. Apache ). We would like to implementing CSP for security reasons on Moodle 4.1.8. However; unsure about the necessary parameters and their impact. So are they any guidance on choosing appropriate parameters without affecting the default Moodle 4.1.8. Note: The local CSP plugin is unstable or not effectively working. So looking for other approach as alternative.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Content-Security-Policy (CSP) parameters for Moodle 4.1.8
ResponsesInList.Text: can you please clarify what you mean by "The local CSP plugin is unstable" ? we have that deployed across a lot of sites and it works really well - it allows you to set it in reporting mode first, tweak the policy so it's only reporting things you want to block and then move it into blocking mode. Here's one example policy - but I would expect it won't work for you straight away and would need some further adjustments: default-src *.h5p.org 'self' blob:; script-src *.h5p.org h5p.org 'self' 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval' data:; font-src blob: 'self' data:; style-src https: 'unsafe-inline'; worker-src 'self' *.h5p.org blob:; img-src * data: blob: 'unsafe-inline'; media-src * data: blob: 'unsafe-inline'; frame-src * data: blob: 'unsafe-inline'; upgrade-insecure-requests;

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Content-Security-Policy (CSP) parameters for Moodle 4.1.8
ResponsesInList.Text: Thanks for following up. Initially, indeed. It works normally with the reporting mode; after fine-tuning one by one (adding, editing, and removing CSP parameters), it resets all statistics. It is reflecting normally and allows me to see the new violation report or statistics. After a few attempts, the statistics did not work or did not display the new statistics. I also clear cache in case there was a caching glitch somewhere, but it did not work either. Finally, as a workaround, I need to remove or uninstall the local CSP and then reinstall it to make it function. So I'm not sure if this is just for me or if others are going through something similar. Fyi: - * and *.* in 'script-src' and other '-src' directives allows execution of unsafe scripts and should be restricted. Thank you!

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Content-Security-Policy (CSP) parameters for Moodle 4.1.8
ResponsesInList.Text: If you've moved into blocking mode then the reports stop being generated because the policy is being obeyed. If you aren't getting reports and you don't have it in blocking mode there could be a syntax issue with the policy you have defined. Yes. I'm aware of how csp policies work, due to the nature of Moodle's codebase you can't apply a completely restrictive policy and the above should be considered as just an example to start with. Some sites will find a more restrictive policy than the example I gave above will work fine.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Content-Security-Policy (CSP) parameters for Moodle 4.1.8
ResponsesInList.Text: I used the Content-Security-Policy on a Linux machine (for example, in an Apache configuration file). You may also use this to apply for on your website. Header always set Content-Security-Policy "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' https://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.7.1.min.js https://cdn.jsdelivr.net unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval'; font-src https: data:; style-src https: 'unsafe-inline'; img-src https: data:; frame-ancestors 'none'; form-action 'self';" Thank you

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: SQL Injection

They can at best report a possible risk, the tool doesn't have enough context of the overall code to understand if that risk is exploitable or not. ResponsesInList.Title: Compliance with GDPR: User data is not completely deleted but quiz statistics are affected.
ResponsesInList.Text: We have investigated the effects of approving Data requests (Data privacy) for user data deletion. A.) After approving the request, and waiting for the process to finish deletion, we notice that not all data is deleted: User personal data, at least firstname, lastname and email, are still in database (table “user”) *1. Data log –The table “logstore_standard_log“ has less rows than before deletion, however, there is still a lot of user-related data – see the picture below after user with id=11 was deleted: 1.) Not all quiz module related data is removed; 2.) Core module logs that it has deleted the grade and what the grade was; then it deletes the user and logs personal data, who the user was etc. B.) Furthermore, we noticed, that statistics (At least quiz statistics) are impacted by deleted user data. If user is deleted (through request), user's quiz attempt is deleted and due to the way Moodle works (recalculates stats from relational data), his attempt is not part of statistics anymore. We believe that this is probably incorrect for a lot of use cases. For example: if a public organization organizes some certification exams, and user request to delete data, his attempt should remain part of the statistics. Deleting user personal data, does not change the facts, how many users attempted the exam, how many passed, how many failed etc. The way we see the problem is that we are obliged to delete the user data on request due to regulation, but because of the way quizzes work in Moodle, statistics are not unreliable and therefore not useful. *2 Any clarifications about these finds would be much appreciated. Maybe we are doing something wrong. *1 Name and surname are examples of personal data ( https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/reform/what-personal-data_en ) *2 Our understanding is that regulation allows to avoid deleting such statistical data: The General Data Protection Regulation ( GDPR ) gives individuals the right to ask for their data to be deleted and organizations do have an obligation to do so, except in the following cases: the personal data your company/organization  holds is needed to exercise the right of freedom of expression; there is a legal obligation to keep that data;

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Compliance with GDPR: User data is not completely deleted but quiz statistics are affected.
ResponsesInList.Text: I still have not find the solution to this problem. If my findings are true, there are hundreds of Moodle installations in-compliant with GDPR. Currently we are considering manually deleting data from the database. Any suggestions or comments are much appreciated.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Personal information retained after user deletion per data privacy request
ResponsesInList.Text: @Aran I have spoken to the development team and the change and retention of the email address in that form is part of the deletion process, and to allow reporting on the completion of deletion requests. It is retained on the basis of "legal obligation", i.e. if it wasn't it would no be possible to report on if a deletion request has been actioned. Andrew Lyons posted some details in a comment on the thread below. https://moodle.org/mod/forum/discuss.php?d=376103#p1548578

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Ri: Re: Fake login attempts
ResponsesInList.Text: Black Hats (BH) are always ahead of White Hats (WH) until WH catch up but then the BH find another way. Hosting on systems where you are not in total control puts you at a disadvantage ... if your provider won't install things like mod_security or mod_evasive. There are some things that you could do ... that will probably lead to some pain at first ... and won't be 100% ... but better than what you have now ... Concepts - block/stop as far away from your server as you can and one might have to also block at the network layer (which might require you to upgrade your hosting to a VPS (un-managed). First, investigate what you can do ... software wise ... research CloudFlare Moodle plugin for Multi-Factor https://moodle.org/plugins/tool_mfa If you had greater control over your firewall, one could put the peskiest IP addresses or range of IP addresses in a drop zone of the Firewall of your server.   That's at the network layer.   It also requires you to do more investigation of the IP addresses and range of IP addresses.   Example: don't think any of your valid students would be using a browser from a DigitalOcean (DO) Server.   If after looking at logs of server you see several coming from DO servers you could block a range of IP addresses that included most DO servers - those bots won't see *anything* of your server (note: they will try proxies at that point). Above takes time and diligence once you begin.  You could eventually get to a point where you only have to work on such stuff once a week! 'SoS', Ken

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Ri: Re: Fake login attempts
ResponsesInList.Text: I recommend you to install fail2ban on your server. It's a software package that scans the logs of your server, searching for failed logins, accessing non existent scripts and various other configurable "mistakes" bots usually make. Based on that, fail2ban will block access for those IP's completely (or only one service) for a chosen time (minutes, hours, weeks, ...) It's not so easy to make it scan Moodle logs, but it's very likely that those bots get filtered out because they try to do loads of other stuff wrong on your machine, not visible in the Moodle logs. If your're interested, I can share you my configuration file - it gives a good idea from what it can do to protect your server. Default settings are not enough.

ResponsesInList.Title: User input is being blocked by Azure WAF
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi, I have a question related to Moodle security and would appreciate any constructive help in resolving it. We have a Moodle deployed on Azure cloud infrastructure with Azure WAF enabled. Like the other guys on this forum, we expectedly encountered the issues where WAF blocks harmless user input when it matches firewall rules. Specifically, we have the following SQL I-related rule triggered in the form /mod/quiz/attempt.php: Message ruleId_s ruleGroup_s action_s details_message_s details_data_s SQL Injection Attack 942480 REQUEST-942-APPLICATION-ATTACK-SQLI Matched Pattern match (?i ?:\\b(? ?:s(?:elect\\b.{1,100}?\\b(? ? ?:length|count)\\b.{1,100}?|.*?\\bdump\\b.*)\\bfrom|to(?:p\\b.{1,100}?\\bfrom|_(?:numbe|cha)r)|(?:from\\b.{1,100}?\\bwher|data_typ)e|instr)|ys_context)|in(?:to\\b\\W*?\\b(?:dump|out)file|sert\\b\\W*?\\binto|ner\\b\\W*?\\bjoin)|u(?:nion\\b.{1,100}?\\bselect|tl_inaddr)|group\\b.*?\\bby\\b.{1,100}?\\bhaving|d(?:elete\\b\\W*?\\bfrom|bms_\\w+\\.)|load\\b\\W*?\\bdata\\b.*?\\binfile)\\b|print\\b\\W*?\\@\\@)|(?:\\W*?\\b(?:shutdown|drop)|collation\\W*?\\(a|\\@\\@version)\\b|'(?:s(?:qloledb|a)|msdasql|dbo)')) at ARGS. Matched Data: insert into found within ARGS:q2330:9_answer: insert into Together with our IT security team, we are looking for a solution that will remediate user input and keep us as secure as possible. In order to disable or make exceptions to WAF rules, we need to collect a body of justifications that Moodle will be able to withstand all the variety of SQLI attacks. My request is to help me compose a list of such justifications. Here's what I already have: 1) double check that we are using the latest version of Moodle and there are no known SQL related security flaws reported in "Security Announcements" https://moodle.org/security/ . I also ask for advice, what are the options in principle to exclude such blocking of WAF requests and whether they are possible without modifying the Moodle core code. Thank you, --Roman

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: User input is being blocked by Azure WAF
ResponsesInList.Text:
WAF is designed to protect simple websites, where all the GET and POST data values are expected to be very, very simple. It is definitely not designed, out-of-the box, to protect sites like Moodle, where people do things like discuss maths. Some of is heruistics are massively over-paranoid. (There was a time when we worked out that the reason a forum post was getting blocked was because the user was trying to post text whic included '1+1'. Yes, really!) So, to use WAF with Moodle, you should definitely expect to have to customise the default ruleset, to disable a number of the exessively broad heursitcs. The way Moodle is coded, you should not need WAF, but if you tame its excesses, it can be useful belt-and-braces extra protection. On our system, the rules we have disabled are: 
```text
              Name: AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet


              ExcludedRules:


                - Name: CrossSiteScripting_BODY


                - Name: CrossSiteScripting_QUERYARGUMENTS


                - Name: EC2MetaDataSSRF_BODY


                - Name: EC2MetaDataSSRF_COOKIE


                - Name: GenericLFI_BODY


                - Name: GenericRFI_BODY


                - Name: GenericRFI_QUERYARGUMENTS


                - Name: NoUserAgent_HEADER # This was breaking Moodle SOAP webservice, where it needs to load its own WSDL.


                - Name: RestrictedExtensions_QUERYARGUMENTS


                - Name: RestrictedExtensions_URIPATH


                - Name: SizeRestrictions_BODY


                - Name: SizeRestrictions_QUERYSTRING




              Name: AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet


              ExcludedRules:


                - Name: SQLi_BODY


                - Name: SQLi_QUERYARGUMENTS


                - Name: SQLiExtendedPatterns_BODY
```
 (If you don't have courses that teach about SQL databases, you might not need that second batch.)

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Extended support for Moodle 3.9 LTS
ResponsesInList.Text: As Gemma explains, Moodle security support continues for 3.9. However, Moodle 3.9 runs on PHP 7.4 as the maximum supported version and not PHP 8.0. This is important because PHP 7.4 security support will reach its end-of-life this month: https://www.php.net/supported-versions.php . There will be no more official or community security updates to the 7.x branch of PHP after this month.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Extended support for Moodle 3.9 LTS
ResponsesInList.Text: Yes, by not fixing MDL-70745 for version 3.9 Moodle HQ sentenced it to death. (It was the original promise.)

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Extended support for Moodle 3.9 LTS
ResponsesInList.Text: Agreed. The policy states, "The maximum PHP version supported for a branch will be the max one achieved along the life of the branch. Usually with .0 releases but may happen later". The life of 3.9 core support was June 2020 to May 2021. PHP 8.0 was released November 2020, same time as Moodle 3.10 and well before 3.11. Support for PHP 8.0 was added only to 3.11.8 in July 2022, a full year and half after PHP 8.0 shipped. Yes, PHP 8.0 was a big leap that took time, but by July 2022 we had known for many months, maybe even a year, that 3.9 would have to serve as the LTS for an extra year of duty due to the extra year for 4.0 work. PHP 8.0 support should have been backported so that 8.0 security support and Moodle 3.9 security support would then end at the same time: November 2023. Effectively, Moodle is behind one PHP version and until it catches up, this security version mismatch issue will continue, thereby negating the whole purpose of extended LTS security support. Moreover, it does not seem that 4.1 is shipping with 8.1 support, so the issue will continue, since as an LTS, 4.1's security support (ending Nov 2025) will outstrip the life of PHP 8.1 security support (ending Nov 2024) by a whole year. The active support for PHP 8.0 ends this month too, as well as security support for 7.4. Yet, we are not on 8.1 yet. Are there plans to fix this security versioning mismatch? There's no point in having an LTS that can only run on PHPs that are out of security support. While it certainly may be true that the security issues of the two are usually not related, the basic fact remains: you can't run a secure Moodle on an insecure PHP. An LTS must be secure until the next LTS is available. If you have to backport to make that possible, then you backport. After all, this is exactly how we handle Moodle security issues: backport. If support for 8.0 was seen as a security issue, which it is, then it should have been backported too. The entire point of having an LTS is to be able extend the time needed to upgrade and often that means to move from one to the next smoothly and safely. This is how it has worked since LTS started with 2.7. But now, with the security scheduling mismatch, In the case of 3.9, we have exactly ONE day to upgrade from 3.9 LTS/ 7.4 to 4.1 LTS/ 8.0 - because 4.1 is now slated to ship the very same day on which PHP 7.4 goes out of security support: November 28.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Extended support for Moodle 3.9 LTS
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Visvanath, I'm not aware that we ever promised to support PHP 8.0 in Moodle 3.9 - it was not declared in the original wiki page . Our policies also state: > The maximum PHP version supported for a branch will be the max one achieved along the life of the branch. Usually with .0 releases but may happen later (we added support for php74 with 3.8.3, or support for php80 with 3.11.8, for example). PHP 8.0 was not released until Moodle 3.9 was in service - not in the life of the development branch. PHP 8.0 wasn't released until 5 months after the 3.9 release. We were not in a position to declare support for PHP 8.0 until approximately June 2022, nearly 12 months after standard support for Moodle 3.9 ended and it had entered security-only support. Whilst we try our best to include support for newer PHP releases, it is often non-trivial to do so, and it is not always possible. Our policies also state that the minimum supported PHP version of a release will be the maximum supported version of the previous LTS release so it is possible to upgrade to 4.1 in the interim.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Extended support for Moodle 3.9 LTS

What that means is that after November 13th 2023 we will no longer include Moodle 3.9 when applying security fixes to Moodle. It's worth bearing in mind that even if it were under security support, we typically bundle all security fixes together and at the same time when we release a minor release, so even if it were under support for longer there would not be a minor release until January 2024 anyway. Moodle 4.1 LTS will be released in the coming weeks, providing just under 12 month to upgrade from 3.9 LTS to 4.1 LTS for those who wish to track the LTS pathway. Other Moodle releases, including 3.10, 3.11, and 4.0 have been out for some time now and there has been ample toime to upgrade to an alternative version in that time.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Extended support for Moodle 3.9 LTS
ResponsesInList.Text: Dan, I respectfully must disagree with the idea that only the wealthy or even "the majority" only deserve security. All Moodle sites deserve security, whether or not they use a Partner or have the IT personnel and resources to manage the security details of Linux distributions with out-of- support PHP versions. Having to pay for advanced knowledge such as this should not be a requirement to keep Moodle secure and has never been. Moreover, sites on the LTS track are not second rate citizens and should not be treated as such, which they are in this case. People require both time and a secure platform to upgrade, especially for such a major upgrade as 4.x that has significant changes. Since it debuted in 2014, that has been the purpose of LTS. While the extra time created by extending the security support window for 3.9 LTS was certainly a good decision, the refusal to make it actually secure defeats the purpose of this extension. When Moodle promises that LTS versions have long term security support, they should actually have it. I also do not agree that features should take precedence over security fixes. "Balance" is for choosing among features, not choosing whether to be secure or not.  Features are optional. Security is not optional. And this was a security issue from the very start. In July 2020, it was announced that security support for 3.9 LTS was being extended by six months (to May 2023, later extended to November 2023) which created a security gap due to the known expiration of PHP 7.4 security support in November 2022. This extension was announced only two weeks after 3.9 had been released: it was not "old," it was brand new and an LTS version. At the moment of this support extension, it was obviously clear that the failure to update 3.9 LTS for PHP 8.0 would compromise its promised long term security. This was not a question of balancing one new feature versus another or fixing old features, it was a question of: Do we make it secure? And the answer was and remains, No, we do not make it secure. There was plenty of time to solve this known security issue because it was still a whole six months in the future, in January 2021 that the Tracker 70745 to start work for adding PHP 8.0 support was created soon after PHP 8.0 was actually released. But by then everyone had known for over half a year when the work started on 8.0 compatibility in earnest that 3.9 LTS needed 8.0 support to remain secure. Moodle decided then - and have continued to hold to that decision despite many community requests - that they would refuse to fix this security issue and knowingly allow 3.9 LTS to become insecure one day during its "security support" period, thus compromising the LTS upgrade path. And now that "one day" is here.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Extended support for Moodle 3.9 LTS
ResponsesInList.Text:
Dan, I don't ever recall disagreeing with you in all these long years on any subject, and for good reasons, but yes, we do disagree on this issue, but I think that is understandable. I hope we don't disagree on other things though. I understand your perspective coming from a key partner, but that is not the only perspective in the community. I have clients in industries with regulatory and legal obligations around security, and this issue has prompted them to move off Moodle - which they can afford to do. For them, this is not a matter of money. The real issue here is trust. Are we no longer in a position to trust that Moodle will make their products secure? Security belongs in core and it isn't in this case. When Martin declares Moodle "free forever," I don't recall any fine print at the bottom saying "*except for security." There are many excellent reasons why people should use the services of Moodle Partners. But having basic security should not be one of them. As you say, developer resources are scarce: and that is exactly what we should judge by. If someone decides that such scarce resources will not be used to make Moodle secure, then there is something seriously wrong with development priorities. Are resources so scarce in Moodle that we can not handle basic security for LTS versions anymore? Then stop making the commitment to LTS security. And don't call it secure when it is not. It seems clear to me that, effectively, this decision was a calculated risk that some Moodle users will be left deliberately insecure in order to spend those
resources on other things. What other things doesn't matter if you are
one of those users whose security is affected. And even if you are not
affected this time, next time the decision is made to forego security
for some, you may be the one affected. What assurance do we have that any future LTS such as 4.1 or 4.5 may not be compromised in security to reallocate those resources elsewhere to work on other things, when schedules slip or priorities or personnel change? None, really, because this has set a precedent. I hope it is not repeated but this is a much more serious issue than disagreements about how buttons look or blocks work. Security is fundamental and compromises of security are too. That's all I have to say on this subject. I appreciate your perspective and taking the time to respond and make me think more clearly about this.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Extended support for Moodle 3.9 LTS
ResponsesInList.Text: Just one last thing... we're mixing a few things here and I want to make sure we're on the same page... 1) Moodle 3.9 security support (supported by Moodle HQ) for 36 months with security updates which has also been extended by 6 months due to the 4.0 release delay making 3.5 years of support for Moodle 3.9, this also matches with several other open source projects that offer LTS versions. I don't think anyone is complaining about that? 2) PHP version support. - PHP supports each of their releases for 3 years (security fixes) - unfortunately the release cycle of PHP and Moodle do not match so there will always be some cross-over and there is usually a decent amount of effort to update a Moodle release to support a new PHP version and it's not always easy to make sure none of this work causes regressions for people running an existing Moodle release - (only the new major release gets the full QA cycle right?) - (I think this is the part we we are disagreeing on.) 3) Distribution LTS PHP version support - many distributions provide backport support for security fixes in their LTS versions - ubuntu provide free support that extends this by up to 2 years for free (their LTS releases are supported for 5 years.) 4) ESM Support for Distributions - many distributions offer extended security maintenance on top of their 5 year free support for a fee allowing you to get security backport support for the o/s (including php) for longer than the 5 years you get from the LTS. Here at Catalyst we run the LTS versions of Ubuntu which allows us to get the advantages of 3 and 4 above. I would highly recommend any organisations with "risk-averse" "don't like change" (I've worked in some of these places, and still work with some of these places) to use both the LTS versions of Moodle and the LTS version of an operating system that matches up with the PHP support required for that Moodle release. (It makes life much easier!) - in fact that ESM maintenance allowed us to run some Moodle 1.9 sites for much much longer than they should ever have been in existence... Hopefully that makes it clear - we're disagreeing on item 2 right? - and items 3 and 4 don't meet your needs so you think Moodle should change it's policies around PHP version support?

ResponsesInList.Title: Gnu Anubis - Any knowledge of this SMTP message submission daemon for GPG?
ResponsesInList.Text:
Does anyone have any experience using Gnu Anubis to apply PGP/GPG encryption to Moodle generated emails?  This would appear to resolve the issue of Moodle not having the ability to encrypt outgoing emails.  Or is anyone aware of an alternative option or approach? As described here: " https://www.gnu.org/software/anubis/ ": "GNU Anubis is an SMTP message submission daemon. It represents an
intermediate layer between mail user agent ( MUA ) and mail transport
agent (MTA), receiving messages from the MUA, applying to them a set
of predefined changes and finally inserting modified messages into an
MTA routing network. The set of changes applied to a message is
configurable on a system-wide and per-user basis. The built-in
configuration language used for defining sets of changes allows for
considerable flexibility and is easily extensible." Thanks!

issues are not published until a patch is in place (for more

ResponsesInList.Title: Location Access
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi, Is it possible to forcefully enable location settings at a system level from within the browser or to check if the location setting is enabled or not at a system level from within the browser. I need to create a location report for assessments which tracks any student within a 20 meter radius of each other which has been done however I've noticed that if the location settings are disabled from within the system but enabled on the browser it does not give an accurate location. So I'm looking for a script which either forces the location setting on or checks the setting and displays an appropriate message. Thank you

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Location Access
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Yusuf, You can request location access in-browser, but you cannot force access - you can imagine the privacy implications if any website could automatically enable that feature, even if a visitor has explicitly disabled it. You can find some information about requesting this access in the Mozilla geolocation API documentation . I don't know the exact assessment/device conditions etc, but a few other important factors to keep in mind that might be relevant: Though you can definitely ask for location access in-browser, it's possible to configure a browser to ignore requests for location access altogether, so students are not guaranteed to see the prompt even if you request it. A workaround for that might be to add a note to the assessment with instructions on what needs to be configured to allow that if it is a requirement for sitting the assessment. You're expecting quite granular location information to get within 20m. Browser location does not solely rely on GPS for its data, but on non-cellular devices such as most laptops, it's a reasonably safe assumption they won't have GPS available, so (in my opinion) you're not guaranteed to have data accurate/reliable enough to check students' exact distance from each other with any certainty. As an example, I tested my laptop browser location and it was off by about 10km. It's also possible for GPS to be disabled on a mobile device even if location access is granted. Location would be calculated from the data available, which could be much less accurate. It's possible to spoof the data points used to calculate location if someone is motivated enough to do so.

ResponsesInList.Title: Privacy: userdata and SCORM
ResponsesInList.Text: Somebody reviewing privacy issues in our e-learning came up with this question: Does Moodle pass any personal user data when launching a SCORM package? Can't find anything on this in the Moodle documentation.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Privacy: userdata and SCORM
ResponsesInList.Text: Typically the SCORM package sits within your LMS and does not communicate externally outside of the LMS so all the data is stored within your LMS. The SCORM standard does allows SCORM packages to request the users id (Moodle passes the username in this instance) and the users name. In most cases - this is just so the users full name can be displayed within the package itself (Hi Dan, welcome to this learning package) and it is not sent outside Moodle to any external system. But.... There are a few edge cases to be aware of. 1) AICC HACP - This is a type of content package that is hosted externally to your LMS - it is disabled by default but if enabled, allows a teacher to add an AICC HACP content package to a course using the SCORM plugin. Usually these are commercial off-the-shelf content packages that you would be paying a subscription license for. AICC settings in Moodle allow you to choose if the username or user->id field is sent in the external request and like mentioned above, it can also request the users full-name. 2) SCORM packages can be developed by anyone external and can include any javascript /tracking codes they want to. If you're familiar with things like Google analytics tracking codes - something quite similar could be implemented within the SCORM package by the SCORM author - This will all be done in the users browser session, so you'd be able to see it in the browser console while watching network traffic, but as the scorm package can access the username and fullname of the user accessing the package, it's possible that the tracking data could send this information to an external site

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Privacy: userdata and SCORM
ResponsesInList.Text: just added that to the FAQ: https://docs.moodle.org/en/SCORM_FAQ#SCORM_Privacy

ResponsesInList.Title: Disabling Cookies
ResponsesInList.Text:
Hi security/privacy forum members! I'm
wondering why Moodle saves Cookies, local storage and session storage
objects on clients that are not logged in upon loading Moodle. You can
check the Cookies etc. in your browser's development tools (shift+F9 on Firefox ) if you visit https://school.moodledemo.net/ for example. Is there a way to disable saving these Cookies etc.? That would be easier for privacy policies, asking for permission first and adhering to General Data Protection Regulation ( GDPR ) and similar laws. Thanks! Lexi

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Disabling Cookies
ResponsesInList.Text:
Hi Lexi, The
two cookies loaded on sites like the School demo site are the session
cookie and potentially a Moodle ID cookie. Some details about both of
those cookies are included in the School site's cookie policy , which is linked in the page footer. The
less important one is the MoodleID, which is just used to retain users'
usernames for next time they want to log in. As mentioned in the cookie
policy, that's safe to remove. I can see that the rememberusername settings exists in Site Administration > Security > Site security settings, which
controls whether the site stores a permanent cookie with usernames
during login. I have not tested it, but suspect that disabling that
feature would avoid that cookie being set. For
the session cookie - although you're not logged in, you are still using
the site as a guest user. The site is not read-only and a session
cookie is therefore still required because there may be things you
interact with that need to be associated with your individual session
(and session cookies are generally how websites achieve this). For
example, this ensures that if you change the language on the site (say,
from English to French), that setting is retained when you navigate
between pages, or if you return to the site later and your session is
still valid. It also means that any preferences etc only impact you, and
not everyone visiting the site as a guest (since they will all have
their own session). Session cookies are also essential for users to be
able to log in, so there is no way to avoid using them. I hope that helps answer your questions!

Things like the language could be saved or asked to get saved after it was changed from the default for example. At login of course a Cookie needs to be saved but only then is it really necessary. ResponsesInList.Title: Cross-domain CORS issue
ResponsesInList.Text: Hey I am facing the issue of CORS in moodle. I have shared the moodle session with another external web app (cross- domain cookies ). and what I'm trying to do is to check session status via a custom API using Axios with  "withCredentials: true" params to send the cookie with a request But unfortunately  i got blocked by moodle 'http://localhost:3000' has been blocked by CORS policy: Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check: The value of the 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header in the response must not be the wildcard '*' when the request's credentials mode is 'include'. Any help would be appreciated.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Cross-domain CORS issue
ResponsesInList.Text: The Same Origin Policy ( SOP ) is the policy browsers implement to prevent vulnerabilities via Cross Site Scripting (XSS). In other words, the browser would not allow any site to make a request to any other site. It would prevent different origins from interacting with each other through such requests, like AJAX . This policy exists because it is too easy to inject a link to a javascript file  that is on a different domain. This is a security risk - you really only want code that comes from the site you are on to execute and not just any code that is out there. The Cross Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) is one of the few techniques for relaxing the SOP. Because SOP is "on" by default, setting CORS at the server -side will allow a request to be sent to the server via an XMLHttpRequest even if the request was sent from a different domain. This becomes useful if your server was intended to serve requests from other domains (e.g. if you are providing an API). JSON with Padding is just a way to circumvent same-origin policy, when CORS is not an option. This is risky and a bad practice. Avoid using this. If you want to bypass that restriction when fetching the contents with fetch API or XMLHttpRequest in javascript , you can use a proxy server so that it sets the header Access-Control-Allow-Origin to *. If you need to enable CORS on the server in case of localhost, you need to have the following on request header. Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:9999

ResponsesInList.Text: 'Bad news' travels fast in student circles!   For many students, hearing that will be enough - but think you still need to look at proxy/moodle server config ways to detect and re-direct or drop or throttle to a creepy crawl as that 'bad news' can wear off. My 2 cents! 'SoS', Ken

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: moodle website crawled by hacker bot and get all content and send it to telegram channel
ResponsesInList.Text: OK. You have an incidence and wants to collect more/stronger evidence. Well, you missed the opportunity. You should have harvested evidence before you blew the whistle. I mean, you should have let this wanna be hacker student run loose and recorded his movements. That is the easiest and the most exciting time, I imagine. But then you can't do it alone. You need the support of your IT staff. For example, temporarily deactivate the proxy and collect the IP addresses of this compromised account. Collect the full web server logs (not Moodle logs) and compare the agents. Correlate what is reaped (Moodle logs) and what later appeared in Telegram. Those are the obvious, layman's methods. For a solid analysis you need to get a forensic expert or the service of another "hacker". But again. Once the incidence is over even those specialists will find little, if your system didn't keep records. That's where the real-time hunt comes in. Why don't you confront the culprits with part of what you have and see whether they confess? If there is an initial No, disclose a bit more and threaten with more to come and be ready to pay a higher price. Anyway, in general, there is a limit to what the Moodlers in the General help forum can or willing to do. So moving the discussion to the Security and privacy forum won't be a bad idea after all.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: moodle website crawled by hacker bot and get all content and send it to telegram channel
ResponsesInList.Text: Agree with Mr. V!   And some additional 'do now!' advice.   Many servers typically keep logs and then rotates them keeping old logs archived compressed - up to 4 old log archives. Download those old archived logs now!   They should be compressed ascii files so all that one needs to do is uncompress and use a Text editor with search capabilities to find specific references. As long as this is going on, be a good time to study current logs and maybe even watch in realtime.   Can do realtime 'watching' with a thing called multitail - commnad line only.  I have a couple of 'realtime' multitail scripts ... 'watchweb', 'watchsecure' are what I call them.   The 'watchweb' shows realtime, access log, error log and referrer log.   There are times when I can see a flurry of un-wanted traffic and can via a drop zone in server firewall, stop that traffic instantly.   The additions to the drop zone can be removed. Once one recognizes the IP address, one can do a tail -f /thelogtowatch |grep IP address to filter. Anyhooo ... 2 cents worth! SoS, Ken

ResponsesInList.Title: SQL injection attacks resulting in Error ID '3'
ResponsesInList.Text: I'm a little worried, though probably shouldn't be.  I don't know.  I'm not familiar with the security side of things yet I'm the only person in my department. Recently we got hit by a lot of very fast attempts at using sql injection through the login page.  It started from 1:19pm and eneded at 1:23 pm filling up 8 pages of logs.  (I'm looking at installing mod_evasive for that issue as they should not have been able to make so many requests so quickly) it started off as just "username" for the username.  Then it got a lot more complex very quickly. An example of some of the attempts were like username union all select null,null,null,null,null,null,null,null,null-- azud What has me concerned though is that if I enter this same thing into the login form the log that results shows "User does not exist ("error ID '1')."  But all of their attempts resulted in "Most likely the password did not match (error ID '3')." I've obviously blacklisted their IP both on the server firewall and in Moodle (overkill I know) But should I be concerned that Moodle returned a different error for them than for me trying the exact same thing?  Is it possible they succeeded in getting information?  None of the logs show what they entered for a password (obviously) I've run the security check, almost everything is good (default role says Critical but I tried the reset and that didn't fix it so I'm not sure what the problem is there).  I've updated all admin passwords.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: SQL injection attacks resulting in Error ID '3'
ResponsesInList.Text: Could you share a clip of web service error logs showing that activity? Also, never use your own workstation/browser etc. for trying out what you saw someone/something try .... it might work or your access (IP address might be blacklisted ... mod_evasive and or mod_security would do that. Use another IP'd machine and some other account. Agree that blocking at firewall and moodle is overkill ... the firewall block is really the one to use as that is at the network level ... not the application level. Hopefully, your server is using firewalld ... adding an IP or a range of IP addresses from the offending network in the 'drop' zone ... means they never see anything of your server again.   Very effective. What I normally do is to do a whois on the offending IP address.   If I see it's a server hosted on Amazon, or M$, or DigitalOcean, etc. I might put into the drop zone a CDIR ... all IP's in a range.   If I see in whois it's a customer from a telco in some country and NONE of my users in Moodle would ever be using such a connection, I actually might put  into the drop zone the entire network of telco. Just be carefull not to block yourself! 'SoS', Ken

ResponsesInList.Title: Complete user delete
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi, We have several sites where we delete users and have the GDPR settings set to automatically create removal requests and also create requests for manual deletions. All processes seem to be running and the status of the request is Deleted. However this user is still present in the mdl_user table. My assumption would be that the user would be deleted entirely? Peter

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Complete user delete
ResponsesInList.Text:
Hi Peter, I think this forum post helps answer your question, in particular the paragraph below (I have underlined the part explaining the user table data): " In regards the deletion of Data Requests, we deliberately do not remove
deletion requests. These are kept to serve as a paper trail that the
deletion was actually processed and this is allowed under GDPR. It falls
under the basis of Legal Obligation as the record is required to prove
that you received, and acted upon the request in accordance with the
legislation. Related to this we do not anonymise all data in the user
record because it is required to identify the user that the request has
been processed for . "

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Safety of Data from Hackers
ResponsesInList.Text: There are books/blogs etc. that discuss the topic ... much depends upon hosting, how hosted, what OS, etc. etc.   If one were to do a little research on data breaches one will probably see of the top 2 reasons, failure to fix or patch a major contributor. What version of Moodle are you running?   Use at least a LTS version that is still getting security updates.   Keep Moodle up-to-date with point releases then - easy to do using Git installed moodle code.  Since Moodle is a bunch of PHP scripts, keep your PHP up to date. When it comes to Moodle plugins , keep them up-to-date. So keep your server OS fixed/patched #1.   Case in point, current concern all over the globe for Log4j vulnerability ... does your server currently use it? By 'data' am assuming DB server and DB's contained therein. Reduce 'attack surface' ... examples: If running DB server on same host as moodle code, restrict the DB server to talk to localhost only.   IF running a dedicated server, consider using PHPMyAdmin only when needed ... otherwise, don't leave it available. Don't run an FTP server.   There are other ways to transfer files.   Don't run a full blown mail server on same server as moodle ... example: Postfix on Linux configured for localhost only can send but won't receive mail. Using ssh to server?   Use an un-assigned high port - not default 22.  Also consider restricting sshd to a specific IP address or IP range (your IP's when you access server).  Same thing for open sourced panels ... like Webmin. Linux distro's usually have an announcements list related to security and updates to systems.   Sign up for which ever is yours. Above are some things off top of my feeble brain! 'SoS', Ken

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Code review scan via fortify
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Syed, Automated testing suites like this do not necessarily detect vulnerabilities, they detect the possibility of something matching a pattern that could indicate a vulnerability. The positive results all need to be manually verified before you can confirm a vulnerability exists. When scanning Moodle, these tools are notoriously innaccurate. I have reviewed numerous reports of this type in the past (totalling thousands of pages), and do not recall logging a single legitimate security issue from their findings. Though the number of matches seems like a lot, one of the key takeaways in my experience is that they'll match against every repeated instance of a finding, for example many pages using some shared code can result in one false positive being listed as hundreds of matches in the report. I would suggest reviewing the content carefully, and if you discover any legitimate issues, report them via our security submission form , which you can find at https://moodle.org/security/report/ . That way, any findings can be triaged and verified through our Vulnerability Disclosure Program, and any confirmed issues can be addressed. As we do adhere to a Responsible Disclosure Policy (which means we do not release security information until a patch has been released), this is the safest way to report any security findings. Please ensure you do not post any potential issues to this public forum. I hope that helps!

ResponsesInList.Title: Getting ClamAV Daemon working in Ubuntu 18.04
ResponsesInList.Text:
This is really a note to self, but I've spent all day trying to figure this out, so thought it might be useful to others. I do have a couple of questions though, so if someone knows about systemd that would be great. Running Moodle 3.4 on Ubuntu 18.04 with apache2. I was getting the following error: 
```text
ClamAV has failed to run.


The return error message was "An error occured".


Here is the output from ClamAV:


/tmp/phpXejPcp: lstat() failed: No such file or directory. ERROR
```
 So clearly a permissions error on /tmp I followed instructions like: add the user (clamav) to the apache group (www-data). No change. Finally got to a setting in systemd: 
```text
PrivateTmp=true
```
 https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/systemd.exec.html#PrivateTmp= (on Ubuntu 18.04 this is found here: /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/apache2.service) This,
it turns out, creates Private dirs in tmp for each service. And for
security's sake, one service's tmp files can't be read by another. So the obvious thing to do is set that to false. And after restarting the daemon and apache2, it does indeed work. But...
doesn't that undo that cross process security feature? I guess so. Does
that really matter? I'm not qualified to say. I'd be happy to hear from
someone who actually knows. So I did a bit more digging, and found that there is another setting: 
```text
JoinsNamespaceOf=
```
 https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/systemd.unit.html#JoinsNamespaceOf= This can be used to join 2 namespaces into a single private tmp area. So, in /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/clamav-daemon.service I set: 
```text
[Unit]


...


JoinsNamespaceOf=apache2.service
```
 (add it under [Unit] if it's not already there) And in /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/apache2.service, I reverted to PrivateTmp=true Restarted services etc and this also works. I would love to hear opinions of which is the best solution, or if I completely barked up the wrong tree. Ta Happy nearly Friday.
